newsitem.title: UK: Halifax to find margins under scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: Halifax to find margins under scrutiny.

text.p: Halifax Plc is expected to report healthy first half pre-tax profits next week, but analysts will be looking closely at whether Britain's biggest mortgage lender is seeing its margins and market share falling.
"Everyone will be looking to see how much of the market share they have," an analyst at one European investment bank told Reuters. "There has been a lot of competitive pressure," he added.
Halifax is due to announce its first set of results as a publicly-quoted bank on Thursday, with analysts predicting pre-tax profits of between 755 and 815 million stg.

Extreme competition between the remaining building societies, the traditional high street banks and new players in the financial services sector is likely to put pressure on Halifax's margins, as has been the case for other former building societies.
One analyst said he expected Halifax to have between 14 and 15 percent of net lending, but if the level falls below this, it will be a bad omen.
Analysts were generally less concerned with the half year results than with Halifax's performance for the whole of 1997. "We are really looking forward to the full year figures," said one.

Goldman Sachs predicts full-year pre-tax profits of 1.525 billion stg and a total dividend of 16.28 pence, while others are more bullish, predicting an 18.9 pence dividend and profits of 1.63 billion stg.
But analysts do not expect any more conversion costs to appear in the first half results, although some expect share register costs of around eight million stg as a result of the float.
Halifax was, until its flotation in June, the largest of the mutually-owned building societies, Britain's traditional home loan providers.
It is now one of Britain's 100 leading quoted companies, ranking in the top tier, with more than three billion stg in cash to fund acquisitions and distribute cash to shareholders.

Halifax's mortgage lending generates around 85 percent of its profit and analysts said it may be able to give more detail at its results presentation of how far it has gone with its diversification plans.

Halifax chief Mike Blackburn said recently the bank was not interested in moving towards commercial banking, but left open the possibility of increasing its regional coverage through acquisitions or "agency" deals and other outlets.
Several of Britain's high street banks have established links with supermarket groups in an attempt to broaden their distribution, while others have set up telephone banking operations.
